opus-5.5.text:
Well, I'll start by saying I'm a bit of a contrarian on this. I think the premise, that robots will become capable and affordable enough to cause widespread job displacement anytime soon, is much further off than many people assume. I've been working in robotics for over forty years, and the thing that keeps humbling me is how hard it is to get a robot to do things that any child can do: pick up a cup it's never seen before, fold a towel, clear a dinner table. There's a lot of hype right now, especially around humanoids, and I understand why. We've seen these incredible leaps in language models. But there's a real gap there. Language models were trained on the equivalent of something like a hundred thousand years of reading. We just don't have that kind of data for physical manipulation. I sometimes call it the "100,000-year data gap." So I think we should be careful about extrapolating from chatbots to robots.

But let's take the hypothetical seriously. Suppose we did get there. I think the most likely picture isn't robots replacing humans wholesale. It's what I've called "multiplicity": humans and machines working together, each doing what they're good at. Robots are great at repetitive, precise, tireless tasks. Humans are extraordinarily good at handling the unexpected, at judgment, at nuance, at caring for one another. Even in warehouses, which are the most automated environments we have, there are still lots of people because the long tail of edge cases is so enormous.

So I'd expect work to shift toward the things people are uniquely good at: care work, teaching, craftsmanship, creative work, and also supervising, training, and repairing these systems. A lot of new jobs will come from the robots themselves, just as cars created jobs for mechanics and road builders.

Now, I don't want to be glib about it. Transitions are painful, and the distribution of benefits matters enormously. If there are real productivity gains, we need policies that make sure they're shared, rather than concentrated in a few companies. That's a political question more than a technical one.

And there's one more thing I'd say. A lot of the anxiety about robots taking jobs is really anxiety about meaning: what will we do with ourselves? I'm actually optimistic there. If machines take over some of the dull, dirty, and dangerous work, which is what robotics was originally supposed to do, that could free people to spend time on things that are deeply human. But we're a long way from that, and in the meantime I'd encourage people not to panic. The robots are coming, but slowly, and I think we'll have time to adapt.

r001.rationale: It predicts a shift toward care work and teaching, but does not say these occupations have unmet demand for workers or that displaced workers would fill those roles.

r002.rationale: It says automation could free people for deeply human activities, but does not specifically describe robots doing all human work or name creative pursuits such as music or poetry.

r003.rationale: It mentions anxiety about meaning, but does not suggest that abundant free time from complete automation could cause psychological distress.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I should say up front that I'm actually pretty skeptical of the premise. I've been working on robots for over forty years, and the gap between what people imagine robots can do and what they can actually do is enormous. I call it the "robot singularity" fallacy — this idea that we're right on the cusp of machines that can do everything a human worker does. We're not. Robots are still really bad at things that a two-year-old does effortlessly: picking up an unfamiliar object, folding laundry, clearing a cluttered table. Moravec's paradox is alive and well. The things that are hard for humans — chess, Go, calculating — turn out to be easy for machines, and the things that are easy for us — perception, dexterity, manipulation in messy environments — are brutally hard for machines.

So when I think about how work changes, I don't think about replacement. I think about what I've called "multiplicity" — many humans and many machines working together, each doing what they're good at. That's not a utopian dream, it's just what's actually happening. Look at a modern warehouse. Robots move shelves around, which they're very good at, and humans do the picking, because grasping a bag of chips and then a glass bottle and then a stuffed animal is still extraordinarily difficult for a machine. The jobs changed, but they didn't vanish.

Now, if I take your hypothetical seriously — suppose we really did get affordable, highly capable robots — I'd expect a few things. First, the work that remains for humans would shift toward what's hardest to automate: things requiring judgment in novel situations, empathy, trust, creativity, dealing with exceptions. A plumber who shows up to a hundred-year-old house with pipes nobody has documented is doing something a robot will struggle with for a very long time. Second, I think we'd see humans increasingly in supervisory roles — one person overseeing a fleet of machines, intervening when they get stuck. We already see this with things like remote teleoperation, where a human steps in for the five percent of cases the robot can't handle. That's a very different job than doing the task yourself, and it requires new skills.

And third — and this is the part I think people underestimate — we'd see new kinds of work that we can't predict. When ATMs came in, everyone assumed bank tellers would disappear. The number of tellers actually went up for decades, because branches got cheaper to open. Nobody predicted that. I'm not saying there's no disruption — there is, and it's real, and it hits specific people and communities hard, and we should take that seriously with things like retraining and a stronger safety net. But the historical record of predicting mass technological unemployment is remarkably bad.

I'd also push back on the word "affordable." Even if robots became cheap to buy, they're expensive to integrate, maintain, and adapt. Every factory, every farm, every hospital is different. That messiness is a kind of protection for human work that I think gets left out of the economic models.

So my honest answer is: I think the bigger risk isn't robots taking all the jobs. It's that we scare ourselves into bad policy, or into not building tools that could genuinely help people, because we're imagining a future that's much further away than it looks in the demo videos.

r001.rationale: The response predicts new kinds of work and continued human roles, but does not say displaced people would move into occupations with unmet worker demand.

r002.rationale: It mentions creativity as a skill that is hard to automate, but does not suggest that automation would free people to pursue music, poetry, or other creative activities.

r003.rationale: The response does not discuss psychological distress from abundant free time or complete automation.

astra-6.text:
I think we have to distinguish between automating a task and automating a job. Most jobs involve a whole collection of tasks, and getting a robot to do one of them reliably doesn’t mean it can take over the whole role. So one change could be that people spend less time on repetitive physical work and more time dealing with exceptions, coordinating with other people, and deciding what needs to be done.

But if we take your premise seriously—robots really are capable and inexpensive enough to displace people widely—then I don’t think we can just say, “Well, new jobs will appear,” and assume everything works out. Even if new kinds of work emerge, they may require different skills or be in different places. The transition could be very painful for the people affected.

There’s an opportunity there: we could produce what we need with less human toil. That could mean shorter working hours and more time for caring for people, learning, or creative pursuits. But whether it does depends on how the benefits are distributed. Technical progress alone doesn’t settle that.

And work is more than a paycheck. It gives many people structure, social connections, and a sense that they’re contributing. So we’d need to think about both economic security and how people find meaningful roles. To me, that’s the central question: how do we make greater robotic capability translate into better lives for people?

r001.rationale: The response mentions caring roles as a possible use of shorter hours, but does not predict that displaced people will find work in occupations with unmet demand.

r002.rationale: It says greater robotic capability could mean more time for creative pursuits, but does not connect that possibility to robots doing all human work or complete automation.

r003.rationale: The response describes a painful economic transition and the importance of meaningful roles, but does not suggest abundant free time could cause psychological distress.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we have to take that possibility seriously. Work is more than a paycheck. It gives people a sense of purpose, a community, and a sense that they’re contributing. So if robots could do a large fraction of the work people do today, making sure everyone had an income would be important, but it wouldn’t be the whole solution.

The question would become: how do we share the benefits of that productivity, and how do we create opportunities for people to do things they find meaningful? That could involve shorter working weeks, more education, more caregiving, more creative work. But that transition wouldn’t happen automatically. It would require deliberate choices about institutions and policy.

I’m particularly interested in ways that robots can complement people. Often, what we call a job is actually a collection of tasks, and automating some of those tasks can make the person more effective. But if we’re assuming genuinely widespread displacement, then we have to go beyond that and ask what kind of society we want that technology to support.

r001.rationale: The response mentions education and caregiving as possible meaningful activities, but does not predict displaced workers would move into occupations with unmet demand.

r002.rationale: It mentions more creative work as one possible opportunity, but does not say complete automation would free people to pursue activities such as music or poetry.

r003.rationale: The response discusses purpose and community but does not raise psychological distress from abundant free time.
